anchors.fact: (Oxford: the Old Tub name "gained some distinction through the late 1800s", F2, so say "by the late 1800s" and no place.) At Repeal, late 1933, aged sixty-nine, he brought his brother Park, Park's sons Carl and Earl, and his son T. Jeremiah back to work (Oxford pdf 1105: "gathered his family"). Cowdery says the brothers and their sons reopened the distillery. F6
anchors.meaning: A place kept for named others, more than one, after everything had stopped. In our words, never the family-tradition line (C5), and never "he alone" (C4).

anchors.fact: Oxford: to his "chagrin" he learned he had lost the rights to the family's old name, Old Tub. Cowdery: there were problems over who owned that name. F8
anchors.meaning: The private wince, in the record's one word for a feeling. The name was lost, not given (C2). Why it went isn't known.

anchors.fact: By the following August building had begun, and distilling started 120 days later (Oxford pdf 1105, F7: say "by the next August" and "about four months", never "summer" or "a new distillery"; Cowdery has it rebuilt). The whisky went out under his own name instead, and soon became the familiar Jim Beam (Oxford pdf 1105; Cowdery). F8
anchors.meaning: **Our reading** (signposted): he carried on without the old name rather than stop, and kept them working. No motive is on record (C8). Never "Colonel" (C6).

anchors.fact: After he retired in 1944, his nephew Carl and his son T. Jeremiah ran the work (Oxford). When the company was sold in the 1940s, the new owners "kept the name, and the family" (Cowdery). F9, F10
anchors.meaning: The promise held past him. Name only these people and these roles (C7). Who owned what stays out (C1).

anchors.fact: "The best-selling bourbon" (Oxford, sources accessed 2021). Beam descendants "still have a large say" (Cowdery, 2024). F11, F12
anchors.meaning: Lets the drink sound worth having. Present tense ("still"), never research talk (Q145, 2026-10-06: "last I read" cut, "today" not added). Cowdery May 2024 is the latest page read, so re-check before publishing. Say "the family's descendants", not "his" (Cowdery counts the whole Beam line).

anchors.fact: Oxford's Jim Beam white label: "a four-year-old 80-proof whisky" (40%), sources accessed 2021 (pdf 1106). F11
anchors.meaning: A named bottle, recommended. Its strength is on the page only as of about 2021, so give a dated or style-level ABV. Substitute: any Kentucky straight bourbon.

anchors.fact: Oxford: the New York Sour is a whisky sour "with a float of red wine layered on top", dating to the 1880s, "first attested to Chicago". It was known elsewhere as a "Southern" or "Continental" Sour and called "New York" in Boston, from 1885 (pdf 1387). *Imbibe!*: "the name it finally settled on after Prohibition" (pdf 96). Oxford's recipe uses straight rye in a cocktail glass. The *Codex* gives it as bourbon, lemon and simple syrup, "shaken and served in a coupe with a float of juicy red wine" (p. 257).
anchors.meaning: Name it as a renowned classic. The name's history stays out: it would be a second name story beside Old Tub. Bourbon is on a page (Codex); the wine glass and the 20 ml of syrup are Tomás's, so never "the classic way".

anchors.fact: An 1883 Chicago bartender told a reporter that "the claret makes the drink look well and it gives it a better taste" (*Imbibe!* pdf 96; Oxford pdf 1387, *Chicago Tribune* 25 Nov 1883). He also claimed to have invented it, and Wondrich is sceptical: another Chicago bartender topped a sour with claret the same year.
anchors.meaning: The proof line, with its channel: "a Chicago bartender told a reporter in 1883". In the epigraph, it's "his sours", never a bare "it" that makes our glass the one he praised. Never "the man who invented it". Our reading: the one thing allowed to show makes the whole better.
anchors.speaksTo: let them see you mind, once

anchors.fact: Oxford: egg white and ice "blur the sharp line" between the sour and the float (pdf 1387).
anchors.meaning: Up, with no egg and no ice. The line stays sharp.

anchors.fact: Tannins in grape skins and seeds give red wine its tannic flavours, and many polyphenols are astringent (*LI* p. 265).
anchors.meaning: A taste claim, labelled as taste: a small dry pucker on the first sip, then the sour.

anchors.fact: The *Flavor Matrix* lists red wine among corn's surprise pairings (pdf 88). Bourbon must be at least 51% corn by US regulation (Oxford CORN pdf 583).
anchors.meaning: The classic float is also the Matrix's pairing, so the classic is kept because the float is the point. Say "bourbon is mostly corn", never Jim Beam's own mash bill (not on a page).

cocktail.closingLine: Float the red so it shows. Once in a while, so should the cost.
cocktail.glassware: small stemmed wine glass (about 250 ml), chilled, no ice in the glass
method: Chill the glass in the freezer, or fill it with ice water while you mix.
Put the bourbon, lemon juice and simple syrup in a shaker. Fill it with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds, until the shaker is frosty on the outside.
Empty the glass. Strain the drink into it, through a small sieve as well, so no chips of ice get in. Let it settle for a few seconds.
Hold a spoon upside down just above the drink, and pour the red wine slowly onto the back of it, so the wine spreads out and rests on top as a thin red layer. Don't stir. No garnish.
cocktail.name: A Place Kept

recipe.item: Jim Beam bourbon (white label, 40% as of about 2021)
recipe.note: recommended: the whisky that took his own name. Or any Kentucky straight bourbon of 40% or stronger
equal parts sugar and water, stirred until clear
a young, dry, juicy red such as a Cabernet Sauvignon. Floated on top, never shaken in

cocktail.tagline: When you say there's room for everyone, there is.

reading.epigraph: Red wine floats on this sour. In 1883, a bartender said wine made his sours better.
whoYouAre: When you tell people there's a place for them, they stop worrying. They can, because you've taken the worrying on yourself. You keep your word the way other people keep a house: every day, mostly unseen, and without asking whether it suits you this week.

You said there'd be a place for all of them. You never said what it cost you. Something of yours goes missing along the way, a plan, a weekend, the thing you'd hoped to put your name to, and you act as if it were the obvious thing to do. Partly because it is. Partly because you're afraid that if they saw you mind, they'd ask themselves whether the promise still holds. It does. Because of you, the ones who rely on you get to stop worrying about tomorrow, and most people go a whole life without that.
yours: Old Tub was a good name for a bourbon. Through the late 1800s it made something of a name for itself, made by Jim Beam's father and grandfather, and in 1892 Jim took over running it, with his brother-in-law. Then Prohibition shut everything down. When it ended, late in 1933, Jim was sixty-nine.

He gathered the family: his brother Park, Park's sons Carl and Earl, and his own son, T. Jeremiah. The family still remembers him telling them it was time they all went back to work. By the next August, building work had begun, and about four months after that the stills were running. Along the way he found out that the right to the Old Tub name had been lost. He minded. The word used for it is chagrin, which is the polite word for a wince. The whiskey went out carrying his own name instead. You've almost certainly seen it.

After he retired in 1944, his nephew Carl and his son T. Jeremiah ran it, and the family's descendants still have a big say in how it's made. We don't know what Jim told them about the name, but I like to think he said very little: there was work to do, and he'd promised them a place in it. I recognise that in you. You keep the place you promised, and when something of yours is lost along the way, you carry it quietly and go on.

The cocktail I've made for you is a New York Sour, a renowned classic. Mine is bourbon, fresh lemon and sugar, shaken cold and poured without ice, sharp and clean. I'd make it with Jim Beam, since it carries the name he ended up with, though any Kentucky straight bourbon will do. Then one thing goes over the top: a float of dry red wine, a thin red band above the tawny sour. Only the wine shows, and it brings a little dry pucker to the bright sour. Back in 1883, a bartender in Chicago told a reporter the wine made the drink look good and taste better. I put it there for the one thing in this story that stung.

One request, then. When keeping a promise costs you something, say so, once, to someone you kept the place for. The promise won't look any weaker. It'll look exactly like what it is: something you care about enough to pay for. And they'll finally get the chance to thank you, which you so rarely allow.
